headline_en: Raising remittances through worker skills development: specific initiatives needed
summary_en: A reader-contributed opinion piece (Dur Porobash section) by Rahman Mridha, a former Pfizer director in Sweden, argues that remittances can grow if Bangladesh sets up corruption-free, international-standard 'special vocational training centres' for current and aspiring migrant workers. It lists occupations he says are in demand abroad, what the government and embassies should do, and proposes minimum education and language requirements for trainees. It contains proposals and general claims, not reported events.

facts.statement: The writer states that at present roughly more than one crore (10 million) Bangladeshis are working in various countries. No source is given for the figure.
facts.source_in_article: Rahman Mridha, opinion writer (former director, Pfizer, Sweden)

facts.statement: The writer proposes setting up corruption-free, international-standard 'special vocational training centres' (বিশেষ ভোকেশনাল ট্রেনিং সেন্টার) to raise the skills of migrant workers and people wishing to migrate; this is a proposal, not an existing scheme.

The writer says skilled, trained workers generally get higher pay, more job security, more chance of promotion and the option of moving between different fields of work, and that technical skill is essential to compete in the international labour market.

The writer lists occupations he says are in demand abroad for Bangladeshi workers if trained: health care (nurses, doctors) in developed countries, needing proper training and language skills; engineering (construction, mechanical, electrical), needing advanced training and international-standard certificates; home and personal services (domestic workers, cooks, beauticians, child-care workers) in developed countries; security guards in various countries, needing training and language skills; and gardeners in many countries of the Middle East and Europe.

The writer claims demand for workers in old-age homes and personal care in China is steadily rising, and that a minimum knowledge of the Chinese language is essential for such work. (He also writes that the average life expectancy of China's elderly is about 100 years; this is the article's own claim.)

The writer claims worker demand in the Middle East is steadily rising and that with minimum Arabic-language skill Bangladeshi workers could work in old-age homes or personal care in Arab countries and earn significantly.

The writer says the government should keep training centres corruption-free through strict monitoring, neutral administration and regular inspection; provide infrastructure, international-standard equipment and trainers; allocate funds and open the way for private-sector partnership investment; and give incentives to workers who take training.

Under the writer's proposal, trainees would need a minimum educational qualification and basic language skill; workers with basic knowledge of the selected language would get priority at the training centre and their language skill would be checked through an internal test.

The writer says Bangladeshi embassies and ambassadors should build relations with host governments to create new jobs, do their utmost to protect workers' rights and give legal help when workers have problems, and build links with local employers as a main duty of the embassies.
The writer calls on the Ministry of Education, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and other relevant ministries to jointly implement the skills-training proposal.

headline_en: High Court order due Tuesday on writ seeking independent inquiry committee into mismanagement allegations (sending workers to Malaysia)
summary_en: On Monday 15 July 2024 a High Court bench fixed Tuesday 16 July 2024 for its order on a writ asking for an independent inquiry committee into alleged mismanagement in sending workers to Malaysia after they had received final clearance. The writ was filed by Supreme Court lawyer Tanvir Ahmed on the basis of two newspaper reports of 2 June. The Deputy Attorney General told Prothom Alo that a six-member inquiry committee's report has been submitted to the court.

facts.statement: On Monday 15 July 2024 a High Court bench of Justice Mostafa Zaman Islam and Justice S M Masud Hossain Dolon fixed Tuesday 16 July 2024 for its order on a writ seeking a direction to form an independent inquiry committee into alleged mismanagement in sending workers to Malaysia after final clearance (চূড়ান্ত ছাড়পত্র).

Supreme Court lawyer Tanvir Ahmed filed the writ attaching two newspaper reports printed on 2 June: one in a daily headlined '20 thousand crore taka looted, breaking the dreams of 30 thousand youths' about the Malaysia labour market, and one in an English daily on the subject 'Jobs in Malaysia: more than three thousand workers did not get tickets because of mismanagement'.
The writ asks for a three-member independent inquiry committee headed by an additional secretary of the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment, and for it to submit a report.
The writ came up in court on 30 June 2024; that day the court told the state side to find out and report what action had been taken on the mismanagement allegations.

Deputy Attorney General Tushar Kanti Roy, for the state, told the court on 15 July 2024 that an inquiry committee's report had arrived, and later told Prothom Alo that the report of a six-member inquiry committee had been submitted and the court had kept Tuesday for its order.
facts.source_in_article: Deputy Attorney General Tushar Kanti Roy

headline_en: How 46 Bangladeshis held captive in the Sahara desert came back alive
summary_en: A column by former army officer Sheikh Masumul Hasan, who served as a UN military observer with MINURSO in Western Sahara in 2004-05, recounts how 46 Bangladeshis trying to reach Europe via UAE, Mali and Mauritania were pushed back by the Moroccan army and held at the Sahrawi People's Liberation Army camp at Tifariti in April 2005. He describes how he collected their details, obtained IOM voluntary return forms and, with UN colleagues, got them repatriated from Mauritania to Dhaka in January 2006, about 10 months later.

facts.statement: On 5 April 2005 the writer, then a UN military observer with MINURSO in Laayoune, was told by phone that 46 Bangladeshis had been detained by the Sahrawi People's Liberation Army in Western Sahara and were being held at Tifariti camp.
facts.source_in_article: Sheikh Masumul Hasan, former army officer and MINURSO observer (first-person account)

facts.statement: The 46 Bangladeshis told the writer they had each spent 10-12 lakh taka and travelled in small groups by the route Dhaka - United Arab Emirates - Mali - Mauritania to Western Sahara; some had left home 4 months earlier and some 12 months earlier, and their destination was Europe.
facts.source_in_article: The 46 migrants, as told to the writer

facts.statement: After the 46 Bangladeshis crossed Western Sahara and entered Morocco, the Moroccan army detained them and pushed them back to the Sahrawi side of Western Sahara, where the Sahrawi People's Liberation Army caught them and held them at its Tifariti camp.
facts.source_in_article: The 46 migrants, as told to the writer

facts.statement: While held at the Tifariti camp the Bangladeshis worked all day in the Sahrawi liberation army camp and got one meal of bread and lentils a day from it; some of them had earlier job experience in the Middle East and could speak Arabic.

The MINURSO chief operations officer told the writer that rescuing and repatriating the Bangladeshis was not in MINURSO's mandate and that the mission could only exchange information; only the Sahrawi People's Liberation Army and MINURSO military observers could go to the place.
facts.source_in_article: MINURSO chief operations officer (a Ghanaian lieutenant colonel), as quoted by the writer

facts.statement: The writer informed Bangladesh Army headquarters and the Bangladesh mission in Rabat, Morocco by email, then with permission of the acting UN Special Representative (a German woman the article names as ইনগুন্দে ফুউলাও) flew to Tifariti, took food, and collected the names and addresses of the 46; he scanned their handwritten letters and had a friend in Dhaka print and post them to their families.

The detained men all asked the writer to help them reach Europe; he told them he could only try for their return to Bangladesh and ask their captors to treat them well, and writes that in the end there was no way other than repatriation.

In the second week of June 2005 the writer met the Bangladesh ambassador at the Bangladesh permanent mission to the UN in Geneva, then kept contact with IOM headquarters in Geneva and the IOM office in Dhaka, collected IOM 'Voluntary Return Assistance' forms, filled them in for the 46 at Tifariti camp, had photos taken and printed (four sets of papers each), and sent all forms to the IOM regional office in Dakar, Senegal.

According to an email of 30 December 2005 from the UN official quoted by the writer, all 46 were to be handed over at Zouerate (জরেট) on 14 January 2006 and leave Mauritania for Dhaka on 15 or 16 January 2006; the writer says rescuing and returning them took about 10 months.
facts.source_in_article: Email from the acting SRSG, as quoted by the writer

headline_en: How many dollars expatriates sent ahead of Eid-ul-Azha
summary_en: Bangladesh Bank data show expatriates sent USD 72.62 crore through banks in the first week of June 2024, ahead of Eid-ul-Azha, a higher daily average than May 2024, when USD 225 crore arrived (the highest in 46 months). The article breaks the week's inflow down by bank type and leading banks, and gives BMET figures on yearly overseas employment and a ministerial statement on total migration since 1976. It attributes the rise to the central bank raising the official dollar rate by Tk 7 to Tk 117 in May.

facts.statement: Expatriate Bangladeshis sent USD 72 crore 62 lakh in remittances through banks in the first week of June 2024, a daily average of USD 10 crore 37 lakh.
Remittances in May 2024 were USD 225 crore, the highest in 46 months, a daily average of USD 7 crore 25 lakh; the first week of June averaged USD 3 crore 12 lakh a day more.

Of about USD 73 crore received in the first week of June 2024, USD 17 crore came through state-owned banks, USD 1 crore through specialised banks, USD 54 crore through private banks and USD 20 lakh through foreign banks.

In the first week of June 2024, among state-owned banks Janata Bank brought the most remittance (USD 6 crore) and Agrani Bank the second most (USD 5 crore 75 lakh); among private banks Islami Bank brought the most (USD 15 crore 91 lakh), followed by BRAC Bank (USD 5 crore 29 lakh) and Bank Asia (USD 3 crore 30 lakh).
Bangladesh received USD 2,161 crore in remittances in fiscal year 2022-23, and USD 2,137 crore in the first 11 months of fiscal year 2023-24 (the article prints the period as 'July-June').
According to BMET, more than 10 lakh workers went abroad in a year for the first time in 2017; more than 11 lakh 35 thousand went in 2022; and more than 13 lakh went in 2023, a record.
facts.source_in_article: Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training (BMET)

facts.statement: State Minister for Expatriates' Welfare Shafiqur Rahman Chowdhury told parliament in May 2024 that 1 crore 63 lakh 12 thousand 324 workers went abroad for employment in the 48 years from 1976 to March 2024. The article adds that many expatriates are returning home 'failed'.
facts.source_in_article: State Minister Shafiqur Rahman Chowdhury, in parliament

facts.statement: In May 2024 Bangladesh Bank raised the official price of the US dollar by Tk 7 in one step to Tk 117; the article says remittance inflow rose because of the higher dollar price.
Bankers think strict action against money laundering and hundi is needed to raise remittances through the banking channel.

headline_en: Banks stop their own incentive on remittances
summary_en: After Bangladesh Bank announced the 'crawling peg' exchange-rate method on 8 May 2024 with a mid-rate of Tk 117 per dollar (previously Tk 110), banks stopped the extra 2.5 percent incentive they had been paying on remittances on top of the government's 2.5 percent. Remitters now get about Tk 120 per dollar; with the banks' incentive it would have been Tk 123. The government incentive stays. Monthly remittance figures for January to April 2024 are given.

facts.statement: Bangladesh Bank announced the 'crawling peg' method for setting the dollar exchange rate on 8 May 2024, fixing the mid-rate at Tk 117 per US dollar; the official rate before was Tk 110.

Banks had been paying an extra 2.5 percent of their own on remittances in addition to the government's 2.5 percent incentive; after the new exchange-rate method they stopped their own incentive. Remittances now fetch Tk 120 per dollar; had banks continued, it would be Tk 123.
Foreign exchange houses have set the price of remittance dollars between Tk 117 and Tk 117.50; adding the government's 2.5 percent gives about Tk 120.

In October 2023 a joint meeting of the Bangladesh Foreign Exchange Dealers Association (BAFEDA) and the Association of Bankers, Bangladesh (ABB) decided banks would give a 2.5 percent incentive of their own on remittances alongside the government's; state banks and some private banks then began paying it, but remittances did not improve much.

BAFEDA chairman and Sonali Bank managing director Afzal Karim said: after the new method we stopped giving the incentive, because with the government incentive alone the dollar price is close to Tk 120; other banks will decide for themselves.
facts.source_in_article: Afzal Karim, BAFEDA chairman and Sonali Bank MD

facts.statement: Bangladesh Bank spokesperson Mezbaul Haque said banks have been advised to stop their own incentive because of the new dollar-pricing method; the government incentive will remain, and the government will decide on it.
Remittances received by Bangladesh: January 2024 USD 210 crore; February 2024 USD 216 crore 60 lakh; March 2024 USD 199 crore 68 lakh; April 2024 USD 204 crore 30 lakh.

headline_en: 'They have killed my boy'
summary_en: The bodies of eight Bangladeshis who died on a boat in the Mediterranean off Tunisia while being taken from Libya to Italy reached Dhaka on Thursday 2 May 2024 on a Saudia flight; five were from Rajoir, Madaripur and three from Muksudpur, Gopalganj. Relatives say brokers packed 52 people into a boat for 30, forced the eight below deck and beat them back when they tried to come up for air. The family of Rasel Sheikh (23) says a local man named Sumon had promised to get him to Italy for 13 lakh taka. Police say no family has yet complained at Muksudpur police station.

facts.date: boat left Libya 14 February 2024; bodies arrived 2 May 2024
facts.statement: Eight Bangladeshis died on an engine boat in the Mediterranean off Tunisia on the way from Libya to Italy; their bodies arrived at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka, at midday on Thursday 2 May 2024 on a Saudia Airlines flight. Five were residents of Rajoir, Madaripur and three of Muksudpur, Gopalganj. One Pakistani national also died, and the local coast guard rescued several people alive.

The eight dead are: Rifat Sheikh (23), son of Dadon Sheikh, Bardia village, Muksudpur, Gopalganj; Md. Rasel (Rasel Sheikh, 23), Fatepatti village, Dignagar union, Muksudpur; Imrul Kayes Apon (22), son of Pannu Sheikh, Goylakandi village, Muksudpur; Sajib Kazi (19), son of Mizanur Rahman Kazi, Kodalia village, Rajoir, Madaripur; Mamun Sheikh (22), son of Yusuf Ali Sheikh, Paschim Swarmangal village; Sajal Bairagi (22), son of Sunil Bairagi, Sendiar village; Nayan Biswas (24), son of Paritosh Biswas (village given as Uttar Para in one place and Kadambari in another); and Kawsar (22), Keshardia village.
facts.source_in_article: Reporter, from relatives, police and local sources

facts.statement: Several young men from Rajoir (Madaripur) and Muksudpur (Gopalganj) left home for Italy on 14 January 2024, flew via Dubai to Libya, and on 14 February 2024 set off from Libya for Italy through brokers on an engine boat.

Relatives said the brokers put 52 people in a small boat that could carry 30. The eight who died were forced below the deck planks; when they tried to come out because of lack of oxygen the brokers beat them and sent them back, and they died of torture and lack of oxygen.
facts.source_in_article: Relatives of the dead, speaking at Dhaka airport on 2 May 2024

facts.statement: Rasel Sheikh's mother Shilpi Begum said the brokers had agreed to take the migrants across the sea in a big fishing trawler, but instead pushed 52 people into the hold of a 30-capacity boat.

headline_en: Job opportunities for skilled workers in four European countries
summary_en: Four EU countries, Italy, Germany, Greece and Romania, have shown interest in taking skilled workers from Bangladesh in six sectors under the EU's Talent Partnership programme, and a roadmap is to be finalised by June 2024. The EU is initially giving Bangladesh EUR 30 lakh to build capacity. The article describes each country's sector demand, what the roadmap will contain, the open question of the recruitment process (Japan's SSW and Korea's EPS are cited as models) and Bangladesh's request that uncertified mega-project workers be recognised.

facts.statement: Four European Union countries, Italy, Germany, Greece and Romania, have expressed interest in taking skilled workers from Bangladesh in six sectors: shipbuilding, textiles and ready-made garments, information and communication technology, construction, tourism and agriculture.

A roadmap for sending skilled workers to the four EU countries is to be finalised by June 2024; Bangladesh and the EU have been discussing legal migration for about two years and held talks in Brussels on 4 and 5 March 2024. An inter-ministerial meeting on the roadmap, chaired by Foreign Secretary Masud Bin Momen, was held on Wednesday 3 April 2024.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Foreign Affairs officials; Foreign Secretary Masud Bin Momen

facts.statement: The EU is initially giving Bangladesh financial assistance of EUR 30 lakh to build its capacity to send skilled workers.

The EU started a specialised programme called Talent Partnership in 2021 to support legal migration to Europe by giving citizens of partner countries outside Europe skills and work opportunities; Bangladesh is one of seven countries under it. The Foreign Secretary called it a pilot project.
facts.source_in_article: Reporter; Foreign Secretary Masud Bin Momen

facts.statement: Italy wants Bangladeshi workers for the ready-made garment and shipbuilding industries.
facts.source_in_article: A senior Ministry of Foreign Affairs official

facts.statement: Germany wants workers from Bangladesh for the tourism and information technology sectors.
facts.source_in_article: A senior Ministry of Foreign Affairs official

facts.statement: Romania's demand from Bangladesh is for skilled construction workers.
facts.source_in_article: A senior Ministry of Foreign Affairs official

facts.statement: Greece wants skilled agricultural workers from Bangladesh.
facts.source_in_article: A senior Ministry of Foreign Affairs official

facts.statement: The roadmap being drafted covers skills development in the six sectors according to the four countries' demand, a database of interested workers, building institutional training capacity, setting training subjects, certification after training, language and way-of-life training for those going to Italy, Greek-language training, and reintegration of workers who return from Europe.

The process by which workers will be sent to the four EU countries is still being discussed with the EU, because of past complaints of workers not being sent legally, going illegally through traffickers and being cheated. A government official said a model could build on Japan's Specified Skilled Worker (SSW) model and South Korea's Employment Permit Scheme (EPS), or the way workers were earlier sent to Hong Kong could be considered; whatever the process, control of recruitment will stay in Europe's hands.

At least 40 thousand workers have worked or are working on Bangladesh's mega projects (Padma Bridge, Rooppur nuclear power plant, metro rail and similar) and have special skills but no institutional certificate, which limits their job market; Bangladesh recently asked the EU that the lack of a certificate should not be a barrier to their getting jobs.

headline_en: One of four hostages in Libya escapes; traffickers move location with the rest
summary_en: Four young men from Raipur union, Anwara, Chattogram went to Libya legally in February 2024 through a local broker for Tk 4 lakh 10 thousand each, were told they had hospital jobs, had their passports taken, and were sold to another gang that demanded Tk 10 lakh ransom each. facts.statement: Four young men of Raipur union, Anwara upazila, Chattogram went to Libya by the legal route in February 2024: Naim Uddin on 14 February and the other three on 16 February.

After the four reached Libya, members of the trafficking gang said they had all got good jobs at a hospital and took their passports and papers; the four were then sold to another gang, which confined them and demanded Tk 10 lakh ransom each from their families.

The gang tortures the young men and sends videos of it to their families, saying they will be killed if the ransom is not paid. A brother said the captives are being hung up and tortured, that the gang's people spoke to the family in Bangla, and that they called every hour on Thursday 28 March 2024 for ransom.

summary_en: A February 2024 report on the newly formed parliamentary standing committees of the 12th parliament finds that at least six committees, including the one on the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment, may face conflicts of interest because members have related businesses. For migration, it notes that committee member Nizam Uddin Hazari is linked to the manpower export business and is listed on BAIRA's website as chairman of 'Snigdha Overseas', and that former minister Imran Ahmad now chairs the committee. The rest concerns other committees and expert comment.

facts.statement: Nizam Uddin Hazari became a member of the parliamentary standing committee on the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment in the 12th parliament; he is reported to be involved in the manpower export business, and the website of the Bangladesh Association of International Recruiting Agencies (BAIRA) lists him as chairman of 'Snigdha Overseas' (স্নিগ্ধা ওভারসিস).
facts.source_in_article: Reporter's review of committee lists and the BAIRA website

Under the Rules of Procedure of the Jatiya Sangsad, no member may be appointed to a parliamentary committee if they have a personal, financial and direct interest in a matter the committee may consider. A standing committee's job is to review its ministry's work, investigate irregularities and serious allegations, and examine bills.

headline_en: 'Father, I am being tortured': body of the girl who sent this message from Dubai has come home
summary_en: A girl from Gazaria, Munshiganj, who her family says was 17 but shown as 21 on paper, was sent to Dubai on a visit visa on 16 August 2023 after a neighbour took Tk 3 lakh promising a hospital cleaner's job. She phoned her father to say she had been sold and was being tortured; she died on 8 September 2023, the papers with the body giving the cause as a fall from height. Her father filed a trafficking and murder case in Dhaka's Human Trafficking Tribunal in late December 2023 naming two women, Farzana and Sohagi; CID has been ordered to investigate but no investigating officer has yet been appointed.

facts.statement: According to the family, a girl from Gazaria, Munshiganj, actually 17 years old, was shown by the broker as 21 on paper and sent to Dubai on 16 August 2023 with the promise of a cleaner's job at a hospital in Dubai; she was not given that job but was sold in Dubai by human traffickers, sexually abused and killed.
The girl's father, a CNG auto-rickshaw driver, said neighbour Sohagi told the family her elder sister Farzana lives in Dubai and could take the girl there for Tk 3 lakh; the family paid this money.

According to the case statement, accused Sohagi used a broker to get the girl's passport made at a Narayanganj address (the family home is in Gazaria, Munshiganj) and then sent her to Dubai on a visit (travel) visa on 16 August 2023.

A few days after reaching Dubai the girl phoned her father and said she had been sold and was seriously ill from torture ('Father, I am being tortured'); he could not contact her again. According to the information that came with the body she died in Dubai on 8 September 2023, with the cause of death written as falling from above.
facts.source_in_article: Victim's father; Jatrabari police inspector Md. Azharul Islam

facts.date: 26 November 2023; body returned first week of December 2023
facts.statement: The family learned of the girl's death only on 26 November 2023, when the father went to Sohagi after failing to reach his daughter; he was not told why or how she died. The body arrived at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka, from Dubai in the first week of December 2023.

In late December 2023 the girl's father filed a complaint case in the Human Trafficking Offences Prevention Tribunal in Dhaka alleging human trafficking and murder and naming two women, Farzana and Sohagi, as accused. The tribunal ordered the Jatrabari police station OC to record it as an FIR and ordered CID to investigate.

Jatrabari police station inspector Md. Azharul Islam said a post-mortem was done in Bangladesh but the report has not come; forensic samples were sent to CID to find out whether the girl was raped before death; and although the court ordered CID to investigate, no investigating officer has yet been appointed. The father says police are not arresting the accused.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Azharul Islam, inspector, Jatrabari police station; victim's father

facts.statement: Accused Farzana, who recently returned to Bangladesh, told Prothom Alo by phone that she had told the girl that her employer (malik) in Dubai behaves well but makes foreign workers do 'bad work', that she had told the girl not to come, and that the girl came to Dubai without telling her; she said her employer later told her the girl had reportedly been killed and she passed the news home.

headline_en: Lure of residence in Canada: 2 Bangladeshis jailed for physical and sexual abuse
summary_en: On Thursday 22 October 2026 the Saskatoon provincial court in Saskatchewan, Canada sentenced two Canadians of Bangladeshi origin, Mohammad (MD) Masum (45) and Sohel Haider (56), for trafficking a Bangladeshi woman lured with a restaurant job and permanent residence through the temporary foreign worker process. Masum got 14 years for human trafficking and three sexual assaults; Haider got 4 years for human trafficking; both must pay restitution for unpaid wages. The woman was made to work six days a week without a valid work permit, underpaid, had her passport taken and was raped, between 1 August 2022 and 31 March 2023.

facts.statement: On Thursday 22 October 2026 Judge Miguel Martinez of the Saskatoon provincial court, Saskatchewan, Canada, sentenced main accused Mohammad (MD) Masum (45) to 14 years' rigorous imprisonment for human trafficking and three separate sexual assaults (rape), and Sohel Haider (56) to 4 years, the minimum under Canadian law, for human trafficking. Both are Canada residents of Bangladeshi origin.
The court ordered Sohel Haider to pay CAD 5,885.16 and Mohammad Masum to pay CAD 12,268 as the victim's unpaid wages and restitution.

A Bangladeshi woman who had worked about 18 years in a government job in Bangladesh was promised a restaurant job in Canada and permanent residence through the temporary foreign worker (TFW) process. After arriving she was forced to work first at a restaurant run by Sohel Haider in the Gull Lake (গিল লেক) area of Saskatchewan and then at Mohammad Masum's restaurant in the Tisdale area.

The accused did not hold a valid work permit for the woman; telling her the permit papers were being processed, they made her work long hours six days a week and did not pay her properly. Mohammad Masum took her Bangladeshi passport and sexually assaulted her several times by physical force, which the judge explicitly called rape.

Later a different work permit was issued in the name of a restaurant in the town of Elrose; after she arrived there, local Canadian citizens who saw her condition helped her, and with their help she escaped the exploitation and sought legal protection.
The victim's name and identity were not published because of a publication ban ordered by the Canadian court to protect legal confidentiality.

In her victim impact statement the woman said the two men destroyed her life, honour, future, family and career, and that rumours about her at home had damaged her family's standing; she now lives with severe trauma and insecurity.

Crown prosecutor Leslie Dunning argued that both accused took extreme advantage of the woman's situation as a newcomer and controlled almost every aspect of her life. (The article's bracketed names here read 'Sohel and Mahfuz', which does not match the convicted Masum; the article is inconsistent.) Judge Martinez said exploitation of newcomers and temporary foreign workers' vulnerability must be firmly suppressed.
facts.source_in_article: Crown prosecutor Leslie Dunning; Judge Miguel Martinez

facts.statement: Members of the Bangladeshi community in Canada welcomed the verdict and said everyone should be more careful about coming to Canada on fake visas or by irregular means out of ambition and temptation.
A linked headline in the article refers to a case against 5 people over visa fraud involving 209 Bangladeshis in Canada (no details in this article).

headline_en: Embassy tells Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia to stay alert
summary_en: In an urgent notice on Monday 12 October 2026 the Bangladesh Embassy in Riyadh told Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia to stay alert, obey local law and Saudi instructions, and avoid risky and crowded places amid the Middle East situation. It warned that recording, sharing or posting information, photos or videos about the situation is a punishable offence under Saudi law, and gave hotline numbers. After Houthi attacks on Saudi airports, flights were halted at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport and one other airport, and several countries issued travel advisories.

facts.statement: The Bangladesh Embassy in Riyadh, in an urgent notice on Monday 12 October 2026, asked Bangladeshi nationals in Saudi Arabia to stay alert, obey local laws and regulations, follow the instructions issued by Saudi authorities, avoid risky and crowded places and take their own safety seriously in the current Middle East situation.

The embassy said that recording, exchanging or publishing on social media any information, photo or video related to the ongoing Middle East situation is a punishable offence under Saudi law; it asked Bangladeshis not to post such photos, videos or sensitive information on Facebook, YouTube, X or any social media, and also not to store them on mobile phones or share them with others.
Bangladesh Embassy in Riyadh hotlines given in the notice: labour matters toll-free 8001000125; passport matters toll-free 8001000126; diplomatic wing 8001000124; death-related hotline +966570212180.
After repeated Houthi attacks on Saudi airports, flights were suspended on Monday 12 October 2026 at two Saudi airports including King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh.

The United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, South Korea, Japan, Australia and New Zealand issued travel advisories for their citizens about travel to Saudi Arabia after the Houthi attacks on airports.

headline_en: China, India and the United States: Bangladesh's risks in geopolitics
summary_en: An opinion column by Dr A K M Ahsan Ullah, a professor at Universiti Brunei Darussalam, argues that Bangladesh should build need-based partnerships with India, Japan, South Korea, the EU, the Gulf states, ASEAN, China and the United States rather than choose one camp. Its migration-related content is commentary: Japan's labour shortage is an opportunity only for skilled, language-trained workers; Gulf relations should move to skills partnerships and state bargaining over wages, recruitment cost and job-change rights; and Italy and Malaysia are named as labour-mobility partners. It reports no events.

facts.statement: The writer states that monthly remittances to Bangladesh were above USD 2-3 billion in various months of fiscal year 2025-26 (no source given).
facts.source_in_article: Dr A K M Ahsan Ullah, opinion writer (professor, Universiti Brunei Darussalam)

facts.statement: The writer says Japan's labour shortage is an opportunity for Bangladesh, but not on the old model of sending unskilled workers: joint arrangements are needed for language, professional certification, behavioural training and pre-recruitment skills verification, including producing skilled carers for Japan's elderly population.
facts.source_in_article: Dr A K M Ahsan Ullah, opinion writer

facts.statement: The writer notes that South Korea recruits Bangladeshi workers and suggests joint training centres in electronics, shipbuilding, automated manufacturing, batteries, information technology and technical education.
facts.source_in_article: Dr A K M Ahsan Ullah, opinion writer

facts.statement: The writer proposes a sector partnership with Italy on legal labour mobility and small industry, and separate mobility arrangements with Europe for researchers, teachers, industrial trainees and young entrepreneurs.
facts.source_in_article: Dr A K M Ahsan Ullah, opinion writer

facts.statement: The writer says Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, Oman and Kuwait are very important for Bangladesh's overseas employment and remittances, but relations are still mainly limited to sending workers, buying fuel and religious contact; he proposes skills partnerships with joint training and certification centres in Bangladesh matched to how many workers each occupation needs.
facts.source_in_article: Dr A K M Ahsan Ullah, opinion writer

facts.statement: The writer says the most important thing with Gulf states is state-level bargaining on workers' minimum wage, recruitment cost, compensation, social protection and the right to change jobs, and that sending more workers is not success if they go indebted, unprotected and unskilled.

headline_en: Malaysia pledges to strengthen good governance in recruiting Bangladeshi workers
summary_en: Malaysia's Human Resources Minister R Ramanan said in a Facebook statement on Monday 22 June 2026 that his ministry will keep strengthening governance so that recruitment of Bangladeshi workers is transparent, fair and ethical. Earlier the same day Prime Ministers Anwar Ibrahim and Tarique Rahman agreed in a bilateral meeting to form a joint working group that will review the existing MoU and serve as the basis for a new one. Tarique Rahman was on a two-day official visit to Malaysia, his first foreign trip since taking office in February.

facts.statement: On Monday 22 June 2026 Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim and Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman agreed in a bilateral meeting to form a joint working group (JWG) so that worker migration from Bangladesh to Malaysia continues safely and to both countries' benefit.

The Bangladesh-Malaysia joint working group will review the existing memorandum of understanding (MoU) on labour and serve as the basis for drafting a new MoU in line with the two countries' current needs.

Malaysian Human Resources Minister R Ramanan (আর রামানান) said in a statement on his Facebook page that his ministry will continue working to strengthen governance in recruiting Bangladeshi workers so the process is transparent, fair, ethical and free of exploitation, discrimination and unethical practices, in line with both countries' commitments.
facts.source_in_article: R Ramanan, Malaysian Human Resources Minister (Facebook statement)

facts.statement: Ramanan said Bangladesh is one of the main countries supplying foreign workers supporting Malaysia's economic growth, and that cooperation with Bangladesh would ensure workers' welfare, safety and rights and help meet Malaysia's labour demand sustainably and responsibly.
facts.source_in_article: R Ramanan, Malaysian Human Resources Minister

headline_en: 2 expatriate Bangladeshis killed in road accident in Saudi Arabia
summary_en: Two expatriate businessmen from Cumilla, Nure Alam (42) and Yunus Mia (43), who ran a business together in Riyadh, were killed on Friday night (15 May 2026) in a head-on collision in the Afif area of the Jeddah-Riyadh highway while returning from Jeddah with shop goods. A Saudi national also died and two others including the driver were seriously injured. The families ask for government help to bring the bodies home; the Cumilla Deputy Commissioner says the expatriates' welfare and foreign ministries handle repatriation and it takes some time.

facts.statement: Nure Alam (42) of Basudai village, Battali union, Nangalkot upazila, Cumilla and Yunus Mia (43) of Basuara village, Sreepur union, Chauddagram upazila, Cumilla, friends who jointly ran a business in Riyadh, died on the spot when two vehicles collided head-on in the Afif area of the Jeddah-Riyadh highway as they returned from Jeddah to Riyadh with goods for their shop. A Saudi national also died and two others including the driver were seriously injured.
facts.source_in_article: Monir Hossain, Saudi-based nephew of Nure Alam; relatives

facts.statement: Both men had planned to come home for the coming Eid-ul-Azha; Yunus Mia had already bought an air ticket to see his four-month-old son for the first time. Yunus was the sole guardian of his elderly parents, three daughters and two sons; Nure Alam's earnings supported a family of six.
facts.source_in_article: Relatives; Omar Faruk Maruf (brother of Yunus); Sumi Akter (wife of Nure Alam)

facts.statement: Cumilla Deputy Commissioner Mu. Reza Hasan said that when someone dies abroad it takes some time to bring the body home, that the expatriates' welfare and foreign ministries make all the arrangements, and that the district administration will give full cooperation to bring the bodies back quickly through the government process.
facts.source_in_article: Mu. Reza Hasan, Deputy Commissioner, Cumilla
